transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

I’m here because my sleep has gotten… really disrupted, and that’s not like me. I’ve always been very disciplined about sleep — I run a company, I’m used to keeping a schedule, shutting things down, getting up early and functioning. But since my cousin died, I keep lying awake at night replaying that night over and over.

And then when I do fall asleep, it’s not really sleep. I wake up at three or four in the morning with these scraps of hospital images in my head, like fragments, and I can’t settle again. So I go into board meetings feeling like I’ve slept in pieces, if that makes sense. It’s starting to catch up with me.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down or losing interest in things you usually enjoy since your cousin passed away?

Yes… I think so, though it’s not exactly “sad” in the way people may expect. I’m functioning, I’m showing up, I’m saying the right things. At the prayer gatherings, for example, I knew how I was supposed to behave — greeting people, thanking them, sitting with the family, letting people hug me. And I did all of that. I don’t think anyone would have looked at me and thought I was being cold.

But inside, it was like… nothing reached me. My nieces were trying to comfort me, and they were being so sweet, really. I could see that. I could understand it intellectually. But I didn’t feel the warmth I normally would. No relief, no sense of closeness, even though I love them. It was almost like that affectionate part of me had gone quiet, or had shut itself in another room.

So yes, I suppose I’ve lost some feeling for things that should matter to me. I’m still doing what I’m supposed to do, but I’m not getting that normal human comfort from it.
Since your cousin passed away, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy, even outside of family or social gatherings?

Yes… although I think the clearest example is still with people, if that makes sense. It’s not that I’m refusing to take comfort, or that I don’t care. I go through the motions properly — at the prayer gatherings, I greeted everyone, sat where I was supposed to sit, thanked people, let them hold my hands. My nieces were especially gentle with me, and I could see they were trying so hard to help.

But inside, there was just no warmth coming back. No relief. Normally I would feel something from that — affection, gratitude, a little softening — and instead it felt like that part of me had gone very quiet. Like I was performing the appropriate response, but I wasn’t actually receiving any comfort from it. So yes, there’s been a loss of pleasure or positive feeling, even in things that should normally reach me.
Outside of the context of your cousin’s death, have you noticed yourself feeling down or emotionally flat most days?

I suppose “emotionally flat” is closer than “down,” at least from what I can recognize in myself. I’m not walking around crying all day, and I’m still doing what needs to be done. But there’s this strange absence inside me.

The strongest place I noticed it was during the prayer gatherings. I knew exactly how to behave — I greeted people, thanked them, sat with the family, accepted people’s condolences. My nieces came and tried to comfort me, and normally that would move me. I would feel their affection, or at least some small relief from being surrounded by people who love me. But I didn’t. I was behaving properly on the outside, and inside there was no warmth coming back, no softening, no comfort.

It’s almost like the affectionate part of me has gone quiet. Not gone forever, I hope, but just… inaccessible. So yes, emotionally flat, especially in moments where I know I should be feeling something positive.
Since your cousin’s death, have you found yourself involuntarily re-living parts of that night, like flashbacks or intrusive memories, even outside of when you’re trying to sleep?

Yes… not exactly like I’m back there completely, but parts of it come into my mind very sharply when I’m not asking for them.

It happens at odd times. If the phone rings late, especially after everything has gone quiet, my whole body sort of stops before I even know what I’m thinking. And then I get this very clear picture of the hospital corridor — the light, the way it felt waiting there, that awful stillness. Or if I’m driving and headlights hit the windshield a certain way on the highway, suddenly I hear the police officer’s voice in my head again. Not just remembering it calmly, but like it pushes in.

I’ll be in the middle of something ordinary and then there it is, very sharp, and I have to pause and steady myself. I usually try to breathe and remind myself where I am, but for a few seconds it feels like that night has forced its way back into the room.

Have you experienced moments where you feel emotionally numb or detached from people or situations that would typically bring you joy or connection, even outside of the context of your cousin's death?

Yes… yes, I think so. The clearest example is still around the prayer gatherings, because that’s where I noticed it most plainly. It wasn’t that people were doing anything wrong — they were kind, very kind. My nieces especially were trying to comfort me in such a gentle way, sitting close, holding my hand, speaking softly.

And I knew how I was supposed to respond. I did respond, outwardly. I thanked people, nodded, let them embrace me, said the right things. But inside, there was this absence. Normally, being cared for like that would reach me. I would feel some warmth, or tenderness, or at least a little relief from not being alone in it. But instead I felt almost sealed off from it.

It’s hard to explain without sounding cold, and I don’t mean it that way. I love them. I knew they were loving me. But I couldn’t feel the comfort of it properly. It was like the affectionate part of me had gone very quiet, and I was just going through the motions of connection without actually feeling connected.
Since your cousin passed away, have you found yourself avoiding places, people, or situations that remind you of them or that night?

I don’t know that I would call it avoiding, exactly. I’ve had to think about that because it’s not as simple as, “I refuse to go here” or “I won’t speak to that person.” I haven’t noticed myself making a clear, deliberate effort to stay away from people or places connected to my cousin.

There are moments where I hesitate, I suppose — where I think, “Do I really want to deal with this right now?” — but I can’t honestly say I’ve been organizing my life around avoiding reminders. If there’s a family obligation or someone reaches out, I generally respond. I may not feel normal doing it, but I don’t think I’ve been cutting people off or refusing to go somewhere because it reminds me of that night.

So… no, not in a strong or obvious way. At least not that I’ve recognized.
Have these symptoms been affecting your ability to function normally in your daily life — for example, at work, with family, or in social situations?

Yes… it has, though I’m still functioning in the basic sense. I don’t want to give the impression that everything has collapsed, because it hasn’t. I’m still getting dressed, still answering the most important calls, still showing up for the meetings I absolutely have to attend. Especially with work, I’ve tried very hard not to let people see too much of what’s going on.

But I’m not as steady as I usually am. That’s the part I notice. I’m normally very good with people — reading the room, listening carefully, making decisions, carrying a lot at once. Lately I can still do it for a short stretch, but it takes much more effort, and I don’t feel as effective. I find myself wanting meetings to end sooner, or needing to be alone afterward just to collect myself.

I’ve also started shortening my workdays when I can. Not dramatically, not disappearing, but leaving earlier or blocking off time instead of pushing through the way I normally would. And there are community obligations I would usually handle myself — calls, appearances, committees, things people expect me to be present for — and I’ve been delegating more of those than I ordinarily would.

So yes, it’s affecting me. I’m still showing up for the essential things, but I’m not operating at my normal level, especially when I have to be engaged with people for long periods.
Have you noticed this emotional flatness or lack of pleasure in things you used to enjoy even during times that aren’t related to your cousin’s death or reminders of that night?

Yes… I think I have noticed it, though it’s clearest in the settings around the prayers and the family gathering afterward. That’s where it struck me most, because normally those are the moments where I would feel something — not happiness, exactly, given the circumstances, but warmth, connection, being held by the family, if that makes sense.

When my nieces sat with me and tried to comfort me, they were so gentle. They were doing everything that should have reached me. And I behaved the way I should — I held their hands, I thanked them, I let them sit close, I responded appropriately. But inside, there was just… nothing much. No warmth, no relief, not that softening you get when someone you love is being kind to you.

It wasn’t that I didn’t care about them. I did. I do. That’s actually what made it feel so strange. I knew, intellectually, that I was loved in that moment, and I knew I loved them back. But the feeling of it didn’t seem to arrive. It was almost like the affectionate part of me had gone very quiet, and I was just performing the shape of being comforted without actually feeling comforted.

So yes, even when it wasn’t the exact moment of thinking about that night, I found myself flat in situations where I would normally feel some closeness or tenderness.
Have you noticed this emotional flatness or numbness in situations that are completely unrelated to your cousin’s death or that night in the hospital?

I’m not sure I can separate it that cleanly, to be honest. The place I’ve noticed it most is still around the prayer gatherings and the family being around me afterward. Those were not exactly “unrelated,” obviously, but they were also moments that weren’t only about the hospital — they were ordinary human moments, my nieces sitting with me, trying to comfort me, people being kind.

And that’s where it felt so strange. I knew how I was supposed to respond, and I did respond. I held their hands, I let them sit close, I said the right things, I think. Outwardly I probably seemed composed, maybe even receptive. But inside, there wasn’t the warmth I would normally feel. There wasn’t that sense of relief you get when someone you love is trying to take care of you.

It was almost as if the affectionate part of me had gone quiet. Not gone completely, because I know I love them, but the feeling didn’t come through in the moment. So if you mean totally unrelated, like some random pleasant thing with no connection at all, I’m less sure. But in those comforting, family moments, yes — I was behaving properly, but emotionally I felt very flat.
